q: How does the PMBOK Guide, Eighth Edition, describe its project management principles?
options: As mandatory rules that must be followed in order
As processes with defined inputs and outputs
As guidance that reinforces mindset and behavior, not prescriptive rules
As a checklist used only during project closing
explanation: The principles are not prescriptive. They are intended to reinforce the mindset and guide the behavior of people involved in projects.

q: How many project management principles does the PMBOK Guide, Eighth Edition, define?
explanation: The 8th edition has six principles. Twelve was the 7th edition; seven is the number of performance domains in the 8th edition.

q: What are the three dimensions of the project management mindset?
explanation: The mindset has three dimensions: proactive, ownership and value-driven. Each groups two of the six principles.

q: Which two principles belong to the 'ownership' dimension of the mindset?
options: Adopt a Holistic View and Embed Quality Into Processes and Deliverables
Be an Accountable Leader and Build an Empowered Culture
Focus on Value and Integrate Sustainability Within All Project Areas
Focus on Value and Be an Accountable Leader
explanation: Ownership is about leader accountability and a high-performance team culture: Be an Accountable Leader and Build an Empowered Culture.

q: What is the relationship between principles and performance domains?
options: Principles describe the mindset; performance domains are the mechanics that put it into practice
Performance domains replace the principles once planning starts
Principles apply to agile projects; performance domains apply to predictive projects
They are two names for the same seven items
explanation: Principles are the foundation and mindset. Performance domains hold the knowledge, processes and methods that operationalize them.

q: Which list correctly names the seven performance domains of the Eighth Edition?
options: Stakeholders, Team, Development Approach, Planning, Project Work, Delivery, Measurement
Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resources, Risk
Governance, Scope, Schedule, Finance, Stakeholders, Resources, Risk
Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring, Controlling, Closing, Tailoring
explanation: The 8th edition domains are Governance, Scope (including quality), Schedule, Finance, Stakeholders, Resources and Risk.

q: A project manager fixes a recurring delay by studying how procurement, design and testing affect one another, instead of pushing the testing team to work faster. Which principle is being applied?
options: Integrate Sustainability Within All Project Areas
explanation: Looking at components and their interdependencies as a system to find the root cause is systems thinking, the core of Adopt a Holistic View.

q: Adopt a Holistic View is most closely associated with which concept?
explanation: The principle aligns with systems thinking: seeing interrelationships in their full context and patterns rather than static snapshots.

q: Midway through a project, a review shows the product will no longer deliver the benefits in the business case, and no adjustment can fix this. According to the Focus on Value principle, what may be the best course?
options: Continue, because the budget is already approved
Hide the finding until the project closes
explanation: If misalignment persists or the project is unlikely to deliver the intended value, it may be best to terminate the effort.

q: A customer orders new software to increase staff productivity. The software is delivered on time, but staff do not know how to use it and productivity does not improve. What does this illustrate?
options: A deliverable can be completed without achieving the intended outcome
The project fully succeeded, because the deliverable was formally accepted
Quality always costs more than planned
Training is never part of project scope
explanation: The software is an output. The intended outcome was productivity. Adding a deliverable such as training would have enabled the higher-value outcome.

q: When can the value of a project be realized?
options: Only at the moment the project closes
Only after the product has been retired from the market
During the project, at its end, or after completion
explanation: Value can be realized throughout the project, at the end, or following completion. The payback period may extend well beyond closeout.

q: Which document gives the project team the justification and strategy needed to make value-based decisions?
explanation: Project justification and organizational strategy are often detailed in a business case, which guides decisions toward the intended business value.

q: According to the Embed Quality principle, quality applies to:
options: Both the deliverables and the processes used to produce them
explanation: Quality concerns both the deliverable and the processes used to achieve it, measured by acceptance criteria, definition of done, fitness for use and efficiency.

q: Which two practices are described as foundational to embedding quality?
explanation: Continuous improvement and waste elimination let teams refine processes, use resources better and meet or exceed target objectives.

q: A team moves testing and quality reviews to the earliest possible point in the project instead of the end. This approach is called:
explanation: Shift-left means prioritizing quality practices as early in the project life cycle as possible, so defects are prevented or found early.

q: Which quality dimension asks whether a deliverable can cope with unforeseen failures and recover quickly?
explanation: Resilience is the ability to cope with unforeseen failures and recover quickly. Conformity is about matching specifications; uniformity about parity across similar outputs.
